35	### Generics and their specialisation
36	
37	- A **static parameter** is a parameter of a declaration filled at compile time or at run time: a type (`List[\T\]`), a number (`Vector[\T, nat n\]`), a boolean, an operator, a dimension. An **instantiation** fills it (`List[\ZZ\]`). Fortress **reifies** generics: a value carries its instantiation at run time, so dispatch can tell `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]` (Steele 2016, slide 41). Java erases them; this is where Fortress departed from Java.
38	- **Specialisation** is a generic declaration beside a special version for one instantiation: `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])`, chosen at run time by the value. Naden's 2011 workshop paper says the library's authors "found it useful ... to define both monomorphic and polymorphic versions of functions" (`reviews/mie-probes/literature.md` § 1). The team's tests and the checker's dispatcher are built for it.
39	- To make that sound they adopted **multiple instantiation exclusion**: no type may be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic ("a rule that forbids multiple instantiation inheritance, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor", `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`; in the checker since 2010-05-28 and as `checkP` since 2010-07-26). The 2012 Types chapter renames it "instantiation exclusion" and adds a `covariant` modifier (`types.tick:322-339`, `:353-372`). Naden: "Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`). The tower breaks it because each level says "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five instantiations.
40	- **Run-time instantiation**: when dispatch picks a generic declaration the static call did not select, its parameters must be inferred at run time; the 2011 paper says so and leaves how "beyond the scope of this paper" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`). Welterweight aims for "the most specific instantiation of an applicable entrypoint" (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`). Steele's 2016 slide 44, "Where We Got Stuck": generic methods with symmetric dispatch need the parametric meet rule and the return-type rule, which need "nontrivial run-time constraint solving" ("a euphemism for exponential cost"); "So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off." Naden's last memo (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/`) restricts the instance by the static return type; implemented on neither path.
41	- **`where` clauses**, a second way to bind a type variable ("Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-352`, and `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, `:384-397`): "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:15`); code generation refuses any declaration with one (FACTS:158).
42	
43	### Overloading and dispatch
44	
45	- Fortress has **symmetric multimethods**: an overloaded call is resolved on all its arguments, once statically (the most specific declaration applicable to the static types) and again at run time (the most specific applicable to the run-time types, `basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The **return-type rule** ties the two: a more specific declaration's result must fit the less specific one's, so the run-time choice never returns something the static choice did not promise.
46	- On static parameters the 2008 release had a first model that "may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented" (the 1.0 PDF, lines 5234-5241). The 2009 draft replaced it with a ban: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ ... Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`basic/overloading.tex:100-107`), and in the same draft listed "Relaxing restrictions on static parameters of overloaded functionals" as future work with Jan Maessen's `array1` pair (`appendices/future.tex:236-266`). The 2011 paper allows differing static parameters under three rules (No Duplicates, Meet, Return Type), the checker enforces them, walk never enforced the ban, and the 2012 restart drops the sentence.
47	
48	### Coercion
49	
50	- A **coercion** is a conversion a trait declares from another type (`trait ZZ64 ... coerce(z: ZZ32)`), inserted by the compiler where no declaration applies without it. It is not chained (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-130`). "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added" (`:454-462`). It is resolved on static types: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically", with an example where `c: C = D` and `f(c)` calls `f(A)` by coercion "despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D)" (`:598-635`). The draft's own example of widths declares `ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` and `ZZ128` from both (`:549-565`); no sentence makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`. "Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values" (`:64-66`), a general sentence.
51	- Numerals: "numerals have their own types ... This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); the types named (`NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`) carry the value and were never implemented; a note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`:83-95`). The prelude has one `IntLiteral`, a sibling each number type coerces from (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390-429`; Maessen 2009: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec"). The interpreter's is `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }` with its arithmetic commented out: "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." (`FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`).
52	- The prelude's coercions are every exact integer pair and none from an integer into a float (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md` § 5, checked at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108`, `:147-149`, `:433-435`).
53	
54	### Sizes
55	
56	- A **`nat` parameter** is a static parameter that is a number: `Vector[\T, nat n\]`. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values. A nat parameter may be used ... to appear in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:78-90`). The library's arrays and matrices carry their sizes this way and their products require the inner sizes to agree (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1680-1684`). The team's checker never checked them ("Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"), the code generator reserved a slot for them (`CodeGen.java:5317-5328`), and the library's `NatReflect.fss:38-40` says of making a size from a run-time number "Really this just proves that it can be done without extending the language. Having proven that, we ought to build it in".
57	- Unboxing (storing a float as a machine double, not as an object) was intended and never built: `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` and the loader's empty "expando" stub (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`).
58	
59	### `comprises` and exclusion
60	
61	- **`excludes`** declares that two traits share no value; an object type excludes every type not above it (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:212-224`). Exclusion is what lets the checker prove two overloads never both apply.
62	- **`comprises`** closes a trait: `trait Number comprises { RR64, QQ, AnyIntegral }` lists the types below it. The draft reads the list at the level of types: the listed traits "are exactly the traits that immediately extend T" (`basic/traits.tex:231-234`, a draft note). The 2012 texts read it at the level of values: an instantiation "is covered by the union of the types in this set" (`types.tick:384-389`); "no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of the comprised types" (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`). The draft's future-work list says "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check" (`appendices/future.tex:285`).
63	- The **self-type idiom**: `trait Ring[\X\] comprises X`, so `Ring[\ℚ\]` "is really just ℚ itself" (Naden, `:576-582`); the patents of 2012-08-31 make it a named exception to the exclusion rule ("Self-types meet"), never built.
64	
65	### The libraries
66	
67	- The specification knows one library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/library/structure.tex:15-18`). The compiler prelude was cut on 2008-12-19 as a "Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (`WellKnownNames.java:110-111`) and grown for three and a half years; the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009).
68	- The library's own flavour: algebra traits (`AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]`), each self-typed, carried by every number type; reductions licensed by associativity and identity; open marker traits (`AnyMaybe`, `AnyList`) with a "not yet" comment where a `where`-clause `comprises` was wanted (`FortressLibrary.fsi:434`). The specified algebraic-constraints library (monoids, groups, rings, fields, `HasIdentity`) exists only commented out (`Library/incomplete/`). Steele's 2016 slide 12 promised "Rational, complex, and quaternion"; only rational shipped.

12	## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says
13	
14	The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:
15	
16	- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
17	- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
18	- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
19	- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
20	- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
21	- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
22	- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
23	- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
24	- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

1	# Multiple instantiation exclusion: the ground for the decision
2	
3	Gathered 2026-09-22 for Pavol's decision after rung P of climb batch 3 stopped: does the compiled path keep the designers' rule that no type may extend two instantiations of one generic? Nothing here decides. Sources are the rung's stop report and judge's ruling on `origin/wip/rung-exclusion-relax` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`, `JUDGE.md`), the papers, the checker, the interpreter, the specification, and seven interpreter probes in `mie-probes/` (each `X.fss` with its capture `X.walk.txt`).
4	
5	Terms. **Multiple instantiation inheritance**: a type extends two instantiations of one generic, for example `object Both extends { Tag[\String\], Tag[\ZZ32\] }`. **Multiple instantiation exclusion**: the rule that forbids this. **A specialised generic overload**: a generic declaration with a non-generic one beside it for one instantiation, `pick[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `pick(t: Tag[\ZZ32\])`. **Return type rule**: when a more specific overload can be chosen at run time, its return type must fit the less specific one's.
6	
7	## 1. The rule in the designers' words
8	
9	- The OOPSLA 2011 paper, `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`: "Fortress imposes a rule that forbids *multiple instantiation inheritance*, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor. ... We call this rule *multiple instantiation exclusion* and adopt it here." A footnote limits it to invariant parameters (`:145-150`). The stated cost is `:154-156`: "easy to enforce statically, and experience suggests that it is not onerous in practice: it is already required in Java".
10	- The problem it solves, from Karl Naden's writeup of 2012-08-31 (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`). The overloads `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\]): List[\X\]` and `tail(x: List[\ZZ\]): List[\ZZ\]` (`:76-81`) are unsound if some `BadList` extends both `List[\String\]` and `List[\ZZ\]`: "at runtime the more specific function for List[ZZ] would be chosen and return a List[ZZ] which is not a subtype of List[String] thus breaking type safety" (`:94-98`). Under the rule such a type "is equivalent to Bottom" (`:344-347`). With the rule in place, the return type rule may trust one instantiation: the rule "rules out any instantiation other than the one known at compile time ... We can therefore trust the instantiation known at compile time" (`:457-460`).
11	- What it costs: "we cannot define hasStringAndInt <: { Has[String], Has[ZZ] }" (`:470-472`). The trade-off is "specialization of generic functions or multiple instantiation inheritance, but not both" (`:477-478`). The outcome: "Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`:496-497`).
12	- The alternatives Naden discusses:
13	  - Filtering at run time by the expected return type, or splitting overload sets per call site (`:241-281`). He rejects both because "programmers can no longer understand the execution of a program without static type information" (`:288-290`).
14	  - Per-trait syntax: "allow some generic traits to be multiple instantiation excluded and others not" (`:475-477`).
15	  - A covariant relaxation that needs a minimal instantiation (`:536-537`).
16	  - The numeric tower, `:568-632`: "This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy" (`:570-571`). He suggests the self type as a bound, `add[\X <: Ring[X]\](X,X): X` (`:618-624`), and ends: "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system" (`:631-632`). The designers left the conflict with the tower open.

37	## 4. The specification
38	
39	- Exclusion is the smallest relation: "the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy all the properties given in those sections (and this one)" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:187-189`). None of the listed properties makes two instantiations exclude (`:163-164`, `:212-216`, `:222-224`). So the type is allowed.
40	- "Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-340`). Its example is covariant (`:349-351`), which Naden's refinement also allows. The invariant cases are `:365-367`, "trait C is a subtrait of *every* instantiation of parametric trait D. Thus, trait C has all of the methods of every instantiation of D", and `:383-397`, `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`. `Empty` is `BadList` written on purpose (JUDGE.md §1).
41	- Overloads share their static parameters: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them. Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-107`). Static arguments are fixed at the call site: "It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site" (`trait-parameters.tex:374`).
42	- In one sentence: the specification allows the type and forbids the specialised overload, which is the other side of Naden's trade-off, and it instantiates at the call site. On the type it agrees with the interpreter. On overloads it is stricter than both paths: the interpreter accepts `MieHeadOrId`'s pair. On inference it differs from the interpreter, which instantiates from the run-time value (`MieInferRet`).

58	- **Java** forbids a class from being a subtype of two parameterizations of one generic interface (JLS §8.1.5), because of erasure. `Integer` and `Long` are flat siblings under `Number`, each `Comparable` to itself only. This is the compiler prelude's tower.
59	- **Scala** forbids it ("illegal inheritance; … inherits different type instances of trait"). Its numbers are flat with implicit widening, and `Ordering[T]`/`Numeric[T]` are type-class values outside the type, so no numeric type extends one twice.
60	- **Kotlin** forbids it ("inconsistent values" for a supertype's type parameter). Its numbers are flat, each `Comparable<Self>`, and widening is explicit (`toLong()`).
61	- **Swift** allows one conformance per protocol. Protocols carry `Self` and associated types, not type arguments, so two instantiations cannot even be written. `Int32` and `Int64` are separate structs under `BinaryInteger`, which is the self type used as a bound (Naden `:618-624`).
62	- **Rust** allows `impl From<u8> for u64` beside `impl From<u16> for u64`. Coherence allows at most one impl per trait and argument list, and the impl is chosen at compile time, so nothing picks an instantiation at run time. Its numbers are flat, with explicit `From`/`as`.
63	- **Haskell** allows one instance per type for a one-parameter class, and many for multi-parameter classes (an extension). Instances are resolved statically. Its numbers are flat instances of `Num`, with explicit `fromIntegral`.
64	- **C#** (not asked for; its generics are reified like Fortress's) allows `IEquatable<A>` and `IEquatable<B>` on one class. Overloads are resolved statically, and generic math uses `INumber<TSelf> where TSelf : INumber<TSelf>` on a flat tower with implicit widening.
65	- What this means for the tower: no peer combines nested numeric subtyping with self-typed traits; every one has a flat tower plus conversions. The peers that allow multiple instantiation choose the instantiation statically, which is the specification's call-site model. Naden's hole appears only with dispatch at run time over reified generics, which is Fortress's combination.

3	# The exclusion fork: a design brief for the route decision
4	
5	## 1. The decision in plain words
6	
7	- A **generic** is a type with a parameter, `List[\T\]`; an **instantiation** fills the parameter, `List[\ZZ\]`. The rule at issue, the designers' **multiple instantiation exclusion**, says no type may be two different instantiations of one generic at once: nothing may be both a `List[\String\]` and a `List[\ZZ\]` (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 1`).
8	- The designers adopted it in 2010-2011 to make one shortcut safe. Fortress lets a generic function have a special version for one instantiation, `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])`, and compiled code picks between them at run time by the value's type. If one value could be both instantiations, the special version could run for a caller who was promised the other type, and the program would go wrong with no type error. The rule forbids such a value, and the checker's return type rule trusts that (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 1-2`).
9	- The collision: the library's numbers nest. `ZZ32` is inside `ZZ64`, inside `ZZ`, inside `QQ`, inside `RR64`, inside `Number`, and each level says "I am `Equality` at my own type" (and ordering, min, max). So one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five instantiations at once, which is exactly what the rule forbids. 61 of the checker's 103 errors on the interpreter's library are this, at 23 declarations (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 5`).
10	- Why it is on the critical path: one library, the interpreter's, is to become the library the compiler checks (`POSITIONS.md:46`). The checker refuses its tower. Rung P relaxed the check alone and found that a program then type-checks and dies at run time, so the relaxation by itself is no fix (`REPORT.md`, "The stop"). One of three things has to give: the rule, the tower's nesting, or the shortcut.
11	- What every route shares: the `DistributesOver` markers go, since they are read nowhere; B and C both need the call-site fix; and the two code-generator defects and the overloading checker's blindness to symbolic operators are holes under every route (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 2c`; `patents-forest-rule.md § 3`; `scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 4-5`).
12	- Route A, keep the rule and flatten the tower to the compiler prelude's shape: no checker work, 14 library headers rewritten, 367 places that rely on the nesting, the interpreter taught coercion (150-200 lines); the error count goes 103 to 22 (`price-keep-the-rule.md`, the short answer).
13	- Route B, drop the rule, make the code generator take a generic's instantiation from the call site (43 lines), and forbid the shortcut by enforcing the specification's overload sentence: 179 library pairs and 12 tests refused under the narrower reading; the count goes 103 to 24 (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md`, the answer; `patents-forest-rule.md § 4`).
14	- Route C, the forest rule of the group's 2012 patents: keep the rule for ordinary generics and let a self-typed trait be carried at several instantiations when they line up by subtyping; about 30 checker lines measured, 40 to 70 derived, dispatch changes unsized, seven library declarations completed; the count goes 103 to 37 (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`, the routes).
15	- A reader who stops here is choosing between: making the library's numbers look like Java's (A); making the compiler follow the specification's model and giving up the specialisation shortcut (B); or building the type group's unpublished refinement that keeps everything (C).

17	## 2. The nine steps, compressed
18	
19	### 2.1 The refresher
20	
21	- A **self-typed trait** takes its own subject as the parameter: `trait Equality[\T extends Equality[\T\]\]`, so `ZZ32 extends Equality[\ZZ32\]` says "a ZZ32 can be compared with a ZZ32". The algebra traits (`Equality`, the orders, `StandardMin`/`Max`/`MinMax`, `Integral`) all have this shape (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 5`).
22	- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs. A **static argument** is the type the checker fills a generic's parameter with at one call; the **call site** is that place in the program. The **return type rule** says a more specific overload's result must fit the less specific one's (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 1`; `multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`, terms).
23	- **Coercion** is a declared conversion the compiler inserts when no declaration applies without it, `ZZ64` declaring `coerce(z: ZZ32)`; the specification uses it between machine widths and resolves it statically (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3-4`).
24

27	- Compiled: refuses the double membership with four errors; accepts the specialised overload and dispatches it correctly; and its return type rule solves for one instantiation only, which is sound only under the rule (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 2`). With the check relaxed, `ProbeMIEPick` links and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` under every placement (`REPORT.md`, "Measured").
28	- Compiled, where a generic gets its instantiation: at the call site when nothing can be dispatched, from the run-time value when it can, and the value records one instantiation per generic, the last listed (`dispatch-and-route-c.md § 1`). Two code-generator defects were found beside this, neither involving double membership: a cast to an uninstantiated return type, and `ZZ32` spelled two ways (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 4`).
29	- Interpreter: accepts the double membership, picks the first-listed instantiation from the run-time value, and can fail at the next typed binding; refuses the Naden-shaped specialisation at load ("non-ground types need exclusion"); on the tower the value's own level wins (`multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md § 3`).

82

84

3	# What the field did with the exclusion trade after 2012
4	
5	## 1. The Fortress type group and Karl Naden after 2012
6	
7	- **POPL 2019 kept the rule for invariant traits and moved the return-type check to run time.** Gyunghee Park, Jaemin Hong, Guy L. Steele Jr., Sukyoung Ryu, *Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance*, Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 3, POPL, Article 11, January 2019, 28 pages, doi:10.1145/3290324, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290324, licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (read here on 2026-09-23 from the Wayback copy of the ACM PDF, http://web.archive.org/web/20240415191855/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324; the full text, read 2026-09-29, is summarised in `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`). The core calculus FGFV has multiple inheritance, variance and reified dispatch. Its [Anc-Same-Trait] rule: "if a class C extends two instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧ … that extends both … because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11). For an invariant T only γ = α = ρ satisfies this (derived here, not stated there), so the invariant case of the exclusion stands, and the covariant case is Naden's "minimal instantiation" refinement.
8	- Its dispatch uses the call's static return type: "[R-Method] seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" (p. 11:17), because "Supporting variance in a type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method invocations at run time" (p. 11:7). This is the option Naden's write-up describes as "The runtime could be enhanced to include return type constraints when considering applicability" and rejects because "programmers can no longer understand the execution of a program without static type information" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:247-253`, `:288-289`). Corrected 2026-09-29 from the full text: the mechanism is the same, but not its role. With the Return Type Rule kept, the check never moves a call away from the most specific declaration applicable to the argument types; it only picks that declaration's instance (Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9, pp. 11:22-23). That is the proposal of Naden's second write-up of the same day, bounds from the static return type added "without changing which function definition will be chosen" (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex:73-80`). It is not the option `justificationOfRTR.tex` rejects, which would have let the static context rule out definitions that fail the rule. His objection still holds for the instance, which the static type can decide (the `append` example, pp. 11:20-21). The paper proves soundness with the ancestor rule in place (sufficiency). It contains no self types and no numeric tower (searched for "self", "comprises", "Integer", "tower"). It leaves out "modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types", which "can be added in an obvious way" (p. 11:25).
9	- Its precursor is in the tree: `Papers/Welterweight/paper.tick:499-509` (Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, Tristan, "PAPER SUBMITTED TO 2012 ACM SPLASH---OOPSLA"). It states the same rule under the name Ancestors Meet Rule, with the reason: "if an object value belongs to one or more instances of some trait T, there is a *unique minimal instance* of T … being able to identify this minimal instance quickly is essential to the efficient dynamic dispatch algorithms we present later" (`static.tick:83-89`). A self-typed-generics step in its dispatch algorithm is commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-212`).
10	- **Four Oracle patents, filed 2012-08-31 (the day of Naden's write-up), name inventors from the type group, Naden among them.** US 8,843,887 B2, *Fast dispatch predicate for overloaded functions with generic type hierarchies that lack contravariance* (Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, Luchangco; granted 2014-09-23; https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8843887), and US 8,898,632 B2, *Dispatch predicate … using type intervals* (…/downloadPdf/8898632). It includes "Minimal instance of generic ancestors: If S<:G[\T\], then there exists U such that for all T where S<:G[\T\]: if G's ith static parameter is invariant, then Ui=Ti", which is the exclusion. It also includes "Self-types meet: if T<:U=S[\U\] and T<:V=S[\V\] then T<:S[\meet(U, V)\] and meet(U, V) must be a declared (not intersection) type. In practice, this means that the instantiations of a particular self-typed generic must form a forest."
11	- The patents define the idiom: "the 'self-typed generic,' where a generic in T also comprises exactly T … Because the only subtype of Comparable[\T\] is T, the two types include exactly the same sets of values, and are in some sense the same type" (8,843,887 col. 6 l. 40-56). The list does not say how "Self-types meet" combines with the invariant clause. 17	## 2. Julia
18	
19	- Single abstract inheritance, concrete leaves. "concrete types may not subtype each other: all concrete types are final and may only have abstract types as their supertypes … It turns out that being able to inherit behavior is much more important than being able to inherit structure, and inheriting both causes significant difficulties in traditional object-oriented languages" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/types/, introduction). The tower is `abstract type Real <: Number`, `Integer <: Real`, `Signed <: Integer` and `primitive type Int32 <: Signed 32 end`, `Int64 <: Signed 64` (same page, "Abstract Types", "Primitive Types"). `Int32` is not below `Int64`. Parameters are invariant: "even though Float64 <: Real we DO NOT have Point{Float64} <: Point{Real}".
20	- The formal account calls it "nominal single subtyping" and says: "There is no notion of soundness in Julia, even for fully type-annotated programs. If a method call does not have a most specific method, a runtime error will be reported. Ambiguity in dispatch is always resolved dynamically." (Zappa Nardelli et al., *Julia subtyping: a rational reconstruction*, OOPSLA 2018, doi:10.1145/3276483, pp. 113:3-4, https://hal.science/hal-01882137/document). The manual's example `g(x::Float64, y)` beside `g(x, y::Float64)` gives "MethodError: g(::Float64, ::Float64) is ambiguous", with the advice "specifying an appropriate method for the intersection case" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/methods/, "Method Ambiguities").
21	- Follows from those two facts (not stated in a source): each type has one declared supertype and invariant parameters, so a value reaches each parametric ancestor through one chain, and `where T` binds from it. Naden's `BadList` cannot be declared, specialised methods beside generic ones are allowed, and no static return type is promised to break.
22	- Why no multiple inheritance. Bezanson's thesis (*Abstraction in Technical Computing*, MIT 2015, https://worrydream.com/refs/Bezanson_2015_-_Abstraction_in_Technical_Computing.pdf) lists "Intersections, multiple inheritance" among features that "would be difficult to add, or possibly break decidability of subtyping" (p. 63). Under "Simulating multiple inheritance" it presents Tim Holy's trait-by-dispatch pattern, noting "The original author of a type like Array does not need to know about this property, unlike the situation with multiple inheritance or explicit interfaces" (p. 74, citing github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/2345#issuecomment-54537633). The manual documents it as "Trait-based dispatch" ("Holy-trait" pattern, methods manual).
23	- Julia issue #5, "abstract multiple inheritance" (Karpinski, 2011-04-27, still open, https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/5), proposed allowing it under one restriction: "If two abstract types are are [sic] used for dispatch in the same 'slot' of the same generic function object then they cannot share a common, concrete descendant". That is an exclusion requirement in the spirit of Fortress's meet rule. It never shipped.
24	- Mixed arithmetic goes through promotion, not subtyping. `+(x::Number, y::Number) = +(promote(x,y)...)` and "the arguments of functions are never automatically converted"; also "although every Int32 value can also be represented as a Float64 value, Int32 is not a subtype of Float64" (https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/conversion-and-promotion/; thesis pp. 90-91). On Fortress specifically: its "coerce feature … a built-in notion of type widening … It is not possible to provide these features in Julia without doing violence to our 'everything is a method call' semantics" (thesis p. 94).
25	
26	## 3. X10
27	
28	- X10 follows Java's rule: "Limitation: A class or struct may not implement two different instantiations of a generic interface. In particular, a class or struct can implement only one function type." (*X10 Language Specification* v2.6.2, §4.6 Function types, p. 48, Wayback copy of x10.sourceforge.net/documentation/languagespec/x10-262.pdf; the same sentence is in v2.1 of 2011-02-23, p. 50, https://www.classes.cs.uchicago.edu/archive/2011/winter/32102-1/reading/x10-latest.pdf). No reason is given.
29	- Numbers are structs, which "do not have superclasses, and cannot extend anything" (§4.2.2, p. 33). Mixing goes through implicit widening: "Byte < Short < Int < Long < Float < Double" (§11.23.2, p. 178). Overloads are chosen statically: "Method resolution is the problem of determining, statically, which method … should be invoked" (§8.12, p. 133).
30	- Its generics are reified (*Fast method dispatch and effective use of primitives for reified generics in managed X10*, X10 Workshop 2012, doi:10.1145/2246056.2246060). The Java back end loses that for one self-typed interface: mapping "x10.lang.Comparable[T] … to java.lang.Comparable … results in the lost of runtime type information for Comparable[T]" (§18.2, p. 244).
31	
32	## 4. The multiple-dispatch line
33	
34	- None of the pre-Fortress systems had type parameters. The OOPSLA 2011 paper says of Dubious, MultiJava and F(EML): "None of the systems described above support polymorphic functions or types" (`Papers/Types/related-work.tick:36`). POPL 2019 repeats this (p. 11:25) and adds that ML≤ "lacks multiple inheritance" and that ParaSail "does not support covariant and contravariant type parameters".
35	- Cecil combined multimethods, multiple inheritance and F-bounded generics by erasing type arguments from dispatch: "Method lookup does not depend on the instantiating types … message sends foo[int]() and foo[string]() will always be dispatched to the same method implementation" (*The Cecil Language: Specification and Rationale*, §4.1.2, http://projectsweb.cs.washington.edu/research/projects/cecil/www/Vortex-Three-One/doc-cecil-lang/cecil-spec-82.html). Its tower puts the self-typed trait at the root only: `extend num isa ordered[num]`, then "num can have subtypes, such as int or float, which can be compared with each other … extend int isa num; extend float isa num; 3 != 3.14 -- legal" (§4.4, …/cecil-spec-86.html). Litvinov's 2003 thesis (ftp.cs.washington.edu) timed out.
36	- Tate, Leung, Lerner (*Taming Wildcards in Java's Type System*, PLDI 2011, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~ross/publications/tamewild/tamewild-tate-pldi11.pdf), the source Naden cites for the unique minimal instantiation: "For Java this invocation is always unique, although this is not necessary for our algorithm" (§4.2, p. 5).
37	- Later work POPL 2019 cites: FHJ (Wang et al. 2018), whose dispatch "uses static types at run time", and Castagna et al. 2015, "a statically-typed calculus with dynamic (explicit) dispatch through pattern-matching" (p. 11:26). No other paper on soundness with multiple dispatch, reified generics and multiple inheritance together was found.
38	
39	## 5. Other languages with generics and one generic interface twice
40	
41	- **Java** forbids it: "different parameterizations of the same generic interface … This requirement was introduced in order to support translation by type erasure" (JLS SE 21 §8.1.5, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html). The reason is erasure, not dispatch. The OOPSLA paper's "it is already required in Java" (`exclusion.tick:154-156`) borrows the rule without that reason.
42	- **C#** (reified) allows it except where two instantiations "may unify for some type parameter substitutions" (CS0695, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/misc/cs0695). Overloads are resolved statically: "Overload resolution is a binding-time mechanism" (§12.6.4.1), and "Static binding takes place at compile-time", except for `dynamic` (§12.3.2) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions).
43	- **F#** 5 added it: "You can now implement the same interface at different generic instantiations" (RFC FS-1031, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fsharp/whats-new/fsharp-50).
44	- **Swift** has no generic protocols, and the Generics Manifesto files them under "Unlikely": "Implicit in this feature is the ability for a given type to conform to the protocol in two different ways" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/docs/GenericsManifesto.md, "Generic protocols").
45	- **Rust** allows `impl From<u8> for u64` beside `impl From<u16> for u64` (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.u64.html) and forbids only overlap: "Two trait implementations overlap when … the implementations can be instantiated with the same type" (Reference, "Trait implementation coherence", https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html).
46	- **Kotlin** forbids it: the supertype closure must be "consistent, i.e., does not contain two parameterized types with different type arguments" (https://kotlinlang.org/spec/type-system.html, "Simple classifier types").
47	- **Scala** refuses it with "illegal inheritance; … inherits different type instances of trait" (compiler message, https://www.scala-lang.org/old/node/3423). No sentence found in SLS 2.13 ch. 5.
48	- **Haskell** allows one instance per class and type: "A type may not be declared as an instance of a particular class more than once in the program" (Haskell 2010 §4.3.2, https://www.haskell.org/onlinereport/haskell2010/haskellch4.html). Instances are resolved statically.
49	- **C++** templates instantiate distinct classes, and overload resolution selects from "a list of expressions that are to be the arguments of the call" (https://eel.is/c++draft/over.match.general). Nothing selects by instantiation at run time.
50	- **Ceylon** (reified, multiple interface inheritance, declaration-site variance; "Like C#, and unlike Java, Ceylon's type system is fully reified") keeps the exclusion for invariant parameters and relaxes the variant ones: "for every invariant type parameter T of Y, the type argument A … given in V and … B … given in W must be exactly the same type, and, furthermore, X is a subtype of an instantiation U of Y such that U is a subtype of V&W" (spec §3.7.2 "Principal instantiation inheritance", mirror http://lucaswerkmeister.github.io/ceylon-spec/html_single/). It has no overloading at all: "Overloading is illegal in Ceylon" (§3.2.1).
51	
52	## 6. The self-typed algebra tower
53	
54	- Greenman, Muehlboeck, Tate (*Getting F-Bounded Polymorphism into Shape*, PLDI 2014, doi:10.1145/2594291.2594308, https://users.cs.utah.edu/~blg/publications/fbound/effing-bound-polymorphism.pdf) identify the pattern. Self-typed traits are "shapes", and "The primary one is to encode a form of self types … useful for binary methods … as well as algebraic operations, such as addition" (p. 3). Their numeric example: with Integer only `Summable<Integer>` and Float only `Summable<Float>`, "the join of Integer and Float does not exist"; under Material-Shape Separation "Summable is only permitted in inheritance and type-variable constraints, not as the type of an expression" (p. 7). A survey of 13.5 million lines of Java found no overlap (abstract), and the Ceylon team found one counterexample and planned adoption (p. 5). The paper does not treat dispatch. It names "type families" (family polymorphism) as the second use of shapes, not the tower.
55	- The flat encodings in current use:
56	  - C#: `public interface INumber<TSelf> … where TSelf : INumber<TSelf>`, implemented separately by `Int32` and `Int64` (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.inumber-1).
57	  - Swift: generic heterogeneous operators `static func < <Other : BinaryInteger>(lhs: Self, rhs: Other) -> Bool`. The proposal "DOES NOT solve the integer promotion problem" (SE-0104, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0104-improved-integers.md).
58	  - Scala: type-class values `trait Numeric[T] extends Ordering[T]` and `implicit object IntIsIntegral` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scala/scala/2.13.x/src/library/scala/math/Numeric.scala, l. 221, l. 67).
59	  - Cecil: the algebra on the root `num` only (§4).
60	- Typed Racket nests the tower statically ("Integer is a subtype of Rational, which is a subtype of Real") with union types and "overloading with intersection types". It names the tower as the hard case for typed languages: "No existing typed language provides as rich a numeric hierarchy nor as many generic operations as those found in Smalltalk, Scheme, or Racket" (St-Amour et al., *Typing the Numeric Tower*, PADL 2012, pp. 1-2, 5, https://www2.ccs.neu.edu/racket/pubs/padl12-stff.pdf). It has no self-typed traits and no run-time dispatch on type arguments.
61	- Apart from Naden's write-up and the 2012 patents, no source was found that treats a nested tower carrying self-typed traits at each level together with run-time dispatch over reified generics.
62	
63	## What the field settled and what it did not
64	
65	- **Keep the rule and flatten the tower.**
66	  - Java, Kotlin, Scala and X10 keep the rule, with flat numeric types and widening. Java's stated reason is erasure.
67	  - The Fortress group kept the rule after 2012 (Welterweight 2012, POPL 2019), for "unique minimal instance" dispatch.
68	  - Cecil's root-only `ordered[num]` and C#'s `INumber<TSelf>` on sibling structs are two flat shapes in use.
69	- **Drop the rule and instantiate at the call site with no specialised overloads.**
70	  - C#, F#, Rust and Haskell allow multiple instantiation, and every one chooses instances and overloads statically. None has run-time dispatch over generic overloads, the one place Naden's hole opens.
71	  - Ceylon allows variant multiple instantiation and has no overloading.
72	- **Neither route.**
73	  - Julia avoids the trade by single inheritance and gives up static soundness ("no notion of soundness"). It keeps specialised methods and moves ambiguity to a run-time error.
74	  - POPL 2019 keeps both the rule and specialisation by checking the static return type at run time, the option Naden rejected.
75	  - The 2012 patents' "Self-types meet … must form a forest" admits the tower's chain of self-typed instantiations inside the rule, close to the review's route C. It was never published, and its test (`comprises T`) is absent from the library's `Equality`.
76	- **Not settled.** Nobody published a resolution of the tower conflict under run-time dispatch, or a proof that the rule is necessary; the published proofs show only that it suffices.
77

3	# The 2012 patents' forest rule for self-typed instantiations
4	
5	Terms as in `../multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`. "Self-typed generic" is the patents' term, defined in § 1.
6	
7	## 1. The rule, verbatim and explained
8	
9	Sources: US 8,843,887 B2 (Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, Luchangco; filed 2012-08-31, granted 2014-09-23) and US 8,898,632 B2 (Naden, Hilburn, Chase, Steele, Luchangco, Allen; filed 2012-08-31, granted 2014-11-25), from https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8843887 and `…/8898632`. The PDFs are scans; the text below is OCR, with the one unclear line (the invariant clause) checked on a 300 dpi crop. Both patents print the same passages. Citations are to 8,843,887, with 8,898,632 in brackets.
10	
11	- **The definition** (col. 6 l. 41-55 [col. 6 l. 46-60]): "A particular idiom used in Fortress is the "self-typed generic," where a generic in T also comprises exactly T. This usually corresponds to a property of a binary operator method such as "Comparable" or "AssociativePlus": `trait Comparable[\T\] comprises T  opr < (self, other:T)  end` … Because the only subtype of Comparable[\T\] is T, the two types include exactly the same sets of values, and are in some sense the same type."
12	- **Meet** (col. 6 l. 58-67): types should "form a lattice, not just a partial order … This requires union and intersection types to ensure that join and meet operations are defined, plus a "bottom" type. … When two types exclude each other, their meet is bottom."
13	- **The restrictions** open "Restrictions on Fortress types include the following:" (col. 7 l. 40 [col. 7 l. 53]). Three passages matter:
14	  - "Minimal instance of generic ancestors: If S<:G[\T⃗\], then there exists U⃗ such that for all T⃗ where S<:G[\T⃗\]: if G's ith static parameter is invariant, then Ui=Ti. if G's ith static parameter is covariant, then Ui<:Ti. if G's ith static parameter is contravariant, then Ti<:Ui. G[\U⃗\] is the minimal instance of G that S extends." (col. 7 l. 46-51 [col. 7 l. 60-66]). Its invariant line is the multiple instantiation exclusion.
15	  - "Self-typed constraints are an exception to this rule; it is permitted to declare that T1<:SomeSelfType[T1]. Because of the different subtyping structure of self-types, this is really more of an equality constraint than an inequality constraint." (col. 8 l. 3-7 [col. 8 l. 18-22]; "this rule" is the order in which constraints are written.)
16	  - "Self-types meet: if T<:U=S[\U\] and T<:V=S[\V\] then T<:S[\meet(U, V)\] and meet(U, V) must be a declared (not intersection) type. In practice, this means that the instantiations of a particular self-typed generic must form a forest." (col. 8 l. 8-12 [col. 8 l. 23-27]).
17	- **What uses it.** Dispatch tests the implementations in "most-to-least specific order … until a match is found" (col. 9 l. 8-11). The applicable one provides "bindings … for any static type parameters" from the arguments' dynamic types (col. 9 l. 30-32). Its `match` step looks for the argument type's instance of a generic: "if ∃ M, A <: M, stem(M) = G, M is minimal then …" (col. 10 l. 16-17). Inference then lifts the lower bound: "else if there are self-type constraints t <: Si[\t\] then search for t' above l such that t' <: Si[\t'\] for all Si; if t' exists then l ← t' else dispatch fails" (col. 12 l. 4-7; prose at l. 33-39).
18	
19	What the words mean:
20	- **Self-typed.** `S[\T\] comprises T`: the instance at T holds exactly T's values. So `S[\U\] <: S[\V\]` whenever `U <: V`, and a self-typed generic behaves as if covariant although nothing declares it so ("the different subtyping structure"). The covariant line of "Minimal instance" then applies to it, and "Self-types meet" is that line plus the demand that the minimal instance have a name. The patents do not say how the two clauses combine; this reading is ours.
21	- **Meet.** The greatest common subtype. For two ordered types it is the lower one; for two unrelated types it is an intersection type, or Bottom when they exclude. "Declared (not intersection)" asks for a named type.
22	- **Forest.** Link each self-typed instantiation to the next wider one a type carries. A forest has no node with two unrelated parents, so each type's instantiations of one self-typed generic form a chain with a least element. That least element is the "minimal instance" the `match` step needs.
23	- **`comprises T`** is the test for being self-typed. Without it, `S[\ZZ32\]` and `S[\ZZ64\]` are two invariant instances, and the invariant clause forbids having both.
24	
25	In plain words:
26	1. Blanket exclusion forbids a type to be two instantiations of one generic: `ZZ32` may not be both `Equality[\ZZ32\]` and `Equality[\ZZ64\]`.
27	2. The forest rule makes one exception: generics that comprise exactly their parameter (`Equality[\T\] comprises T`), whose instance at a type is that type.
28	3. For those, a type may carry several instantiations when they line up by subtyping. `ZZ32` may be `Equality` at `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `Number`, because `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: QQ <: Number`.
29	4. The lowest of them is unique. Run-time dispatch binds the parameter to it: `ZZ32` for a `ZZ32` value.
30	5. Still forbidden: two unrelated instantiations of a self-typed generic, such as one type carrying `Equality[\ZZ64\]` and `Equality[\NN64\]`, unless a declared type below both is also carried.
31	6. Still forbidden: two instantiations of a generic that is not self-typed. `BadList extends { List[\String\], List[\ZZ\] }` stays illegal, so Naden's `tail[\X\]` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])` keeps its guarantee.
32	7. `Both extends { Tag[\String\], Tag[\ZZ32\] }` (`ProbeMIEPick`) stays illegal twice over: `Tag` is not self-typed, and `String` and `ZZ32` are unrelated.

53	## 3. Soundness under it, and the probe
54	
55	**What the minimal instantiation does and does not do.** In the patents it binds a generic's parameter inside the implementation that dispatch has already chosen (col. 10 l. 16-17, col. 12 l. 4-7). Which implementation runs is decided before that, by testing them "most-to-least specific" (col. 9 l. 8-11). A specialisation `f(x: Eq[\Mid\]): Mid` is more specific than `f[\X\](x: Eq[\X\]): X`, so it runs for every value that is an `Eq[\Mid\]`, a `Narrow` included.
56	
57	**In Naden's terms.** `tail(List[\ZZ\])` is safe because no value is a `List[\ZZ\]` and a `List[\String\]` at once. On a forest every `Narrow` is an `Eq[\Mid\]` and an `Eq[\Narrow\]` at once: a legal `BadList`, ordered. Callers typed at `Mid` or above are safe, since the specialisation's `Mid` fits `X = Mid` or `X = Wide`. A caller the checker types at `X = Narrow` is promised a `Narrow` and gets `M`. That caller exists whenever the argument's static type does not show that it is an `Eq[\Mid\]`: a variable of type `Eq[\Narrow\]`, or any generic code over `T extends Eq[\T\]`. The checker's return type rule does not see it. It solves one instantiation (`OverloadingOracle.scala:88`, giving `X = Mid`) and checks that one arrow (`:97`), which is sound only when no value has a second instantiation. So a forest keeps a specialisation sound only if the return type rule checks every self-typed level below it, and (from `ForestTowerC` under `cov` below) only if the checker's static choice and the dispatcher's order agree when a generic's lower instance is more specific than the specialisation. A specialisation at a leaf of the forest, with no self-typed level below, passes. A specialisation at an inner level passes only if every level below has its own, more specific declaration. The patents state no such rule; it is derived here from the probes.
58	
59	**The probes** (`forest/`, run by `forest-run.sh`; walk on the interpreter, compiled under `-Dprobe.rungP=off`, `hier`, and the forest shadow `-Dprobe.forest=fbound`):
60	- `ForestInfer`, the generic alone, returning `Marker[\X\]` for an `N` reached through each static type. Walk gives `Marker[Narrow]` for all six, the minimal instance from the run-time value (`ForestInfer.walk.txt:2-7`). Compiled under the forest shadow gives `Marker[Wide]` through `Narrow`, `Mid` and `Wide` variables and the variable's own level through `Eq[·]` variables (`ForestInfer.compiled.txt:40-45`): the call is not dispatched, so the checker's static argument is used, and its inference picks the top of the chain. Under `off` and `hier` the calls through `Eq[\Narrow\]` and `Eq[\Mid\]` do not check at all ("… is not applicable to an argument of type Eq[\Narrow\]"): outside the hierarchy check the blanket rule still applies to `Narrow`'s two instantiations (not traced further).
61	- `ForestTower`, the pair of `f` called for `N` through `Narrow`, `Mid`, `Eq[\Mid\]`, `Wide`, `Eq[\Wide\]`, and last through `Eq[\Narrow\]`. Walk refuses the pair at load: "with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (`ForestTower.walk.txt:2-6`), as it refuses `ProbeMIEPick`. Compiled under the forest shadow, the first five calls print `M`: the specialisation runs for `N` through every static type. The last, through `Eq[\Narrow\]`, is checked as the generic at `X = Narrow` and dies: "IncompatibleClassChangeError: Class ForestTower$M does not implement the requested interface ForestTower$Narrow" (`ForestTower.compiled.txt:38-46`).
62	- `ForestTowerC` is `ForestTower` with the patents' `comprises T`. Compiled, the output is identical (`ForestTowerC.compiled.txt:38-46`): the checker does not use the clause to place `Eq[\Narrow\]` below `Eq[\Mid\]`. Walk overflows the stack (`ForestTowerC.walk.txt:2`); `ForestTowerCNoSpec`, the same program with the specialisation renamed, runs (`ForestTowerCNoSpec.walk.txt:2-9`), so the overflow is in the interpreter's check of the overloaded pair. Under the shadow's `cov` mode (see `ForestGenericLeaf`) the first call, `f(n)` through a `Narrow` variable, already dies the same way (`ForestTowerC.compiled.txt:48-53`). The reading that fits (the checker's choice was not printed): the checker now finds the generic's instance at `Narrow` more specific than the specialisation at `Mid` and promises a `Narrow`, while the dispatcher still tries the specialisation first, since it orders declarations, as the patents' does (col. 9 l. 8-11).
63	- `ForestGeneric`: `h[\T extends Eq[\T\]\](x: T): T = f(x)`, with `comprises T`. `h[\Wide\](N)` and `h[\Mid\](N)` give `M`; `h[\Narrow\](N)` dies with the same error (`ForestGeneric.compiled.txt:4-7`), and the same under `cov` (`:12-15`). So for a chain the compiled run time already does minimal-instance dispatch, as the interpreter does, because each level lists its own instantiation directly; undispatched calls take the call site's argument instead. Where the result holds the parameter invariantly, as `Marker[\X\]` does, the arm's `Marker[\Narrow\]` then breaks a call site's `Marker[\Wide\]` (not probed through dispatch on a chain). 77	## 5. The Welterweight draft and POPL 2019
78	
79	The draft states the ancestors rule in meet form, not the forest condition. `Papers/Welterweight/static.tick:83-89`: "if a trait extends (directly or indirectly) two different instances T⟦α⟧ and T⟦η⟧ of the same trait T, then it must extend some instance T⟦γ⟧ of T (which could be T⟦α⟧, T⟦η⟧, or a third instance) such that T⟦γ⟧ is a subtype of T⟦α⟧ and also a subtype of T⟦η⟧. A consequence is that if an object value belongs to one or more instances of some trait T, there is a *unique minimal instance* of T to which it belongs." Its rule `[Anc-Same-Trait]` (`fig-meetrule.tick:111-116`) relates instances only through declared variance (`grammar.tick:48-49`), and the draft has no `comprises T` self types. For an invariant trait that forces α = η, the blanket rule. It is the patents' "Minimal instance of generic ancestors" clause, for all three variances. The self-typed part survives only as a commented-out dispatch step, "%\subsection{Self-typed generics}" with "search for $t'$ above $l$ such that $t' <: S_i\OBR{t'}$ for all $S_i$" (`dispatch.tick:195-212`). That is the patents' col. 12 l. 4-7 word for word, without the restriction that makes it well defined. POPL 2019's `[Anc-Same-Trait]` is the same rule and has no self types (`literature.md` § 1).

3	# The price of keeping the rule: the tower flattened, what depends on the nesting, what the interpreter needs
4	
5	Terms.
6	- **Nested tower**: today's library. `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number`, and each level carries the self-typed algebra traits at its own type.
7	- **Flat tower**: the compiler prelude's shape. The numeric types are siblings under a `Number` without algebra, and widening is a `coerce` declaration.
8	- **Leaf**: the tower type an object belongs to directly: `Int` and `IntLiteral` → `ZZ32`, `Long` → `ZZ64`, `BigNum` → `ZZ`, `UnsignedLong` → `NN64`, `Ratio` → `QQ`, `Float` and `FloatLiteral` → `RR64`.
9	- **Dependent site**: a place in a program where a type check passes only because of the nesting.
10	
11	**The short answer.**
12	- **The flat tower is 14 declaration headers** in the library's four core files (§ 1). The 10 objects that only inherit an instantiation keep their text. The algebra moves to the leaves, widening becomes `coerce`, and `Number`'s catch-alls go.
13	- **The nesting carries weight under walk.** A run-time survey over the 392 test files finds 235 dependent sites in 19 library files and 994 in the text of 75 test files (§ 2).
14	  - 160 of the library sites and 207 of the test sites certainly need a conversion.
15	  - 15 inherited methods need restating on the leaves.
16	  - One library line, `FortressLibrary.fss:4121`, is reached by every test expected to pass.
17	- **The interpreter has no coercion, but its phase order already turns every `coerce` into a callable `coerce_<trait>`** (§ 3). Calling them at dispatch and at typed bindings is about 150-200 lines in six files. It would resolve coercions at run time, where the specification resolves them statically.
18	- **Converting by hand instead** means the sites counted above, and the same again in every new program.
19	- **The compiled side's own tests widen by coercion, never by hand.**
20	- **The flat tower takes the checker count from 103 to 22** (§ 5): all 61 exclusion errors go. The count is still masked by `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`, and it does not reach the library's bodies.

22	## 1. What "flat" means for this library
23	
24	The rule only bites where a type adds its own instantiation of a self-typed trait below a type that already has one. `ZZ32 extends ZZ64` is refused because `ZZ32` adds `Integral[\ZZ32\]` beside `ZZ64`'s `Integral[\ZZ64\]`. An object that adds nothing is legal under the rule: `Int extends ZZ32`, `Long`, `UnsignedLong`, `IntLiteral`, `BigNum`, and also `RR32 extends RR64`. So 14 declaration headers change. 12 of them are among the review's 23 declarations with errors (§ 5 there): all but the 10 objects and `Maybe`, whose errors go with `AnyMaybe`'s fix. The other two are `Number` and `RR64`, which have no errors but must take or give up the algebra. The 10 objects and `Maybe` keep their text. The rewrite is `keep/flat-tower-sketch.fsi`, and `keep/make-flat-lib.py` applies exactly those headers to copies.
25	- **The `extends` clauses that go**: `Number extends` its four self-typed traits, `QQ extends RR64`, `AnyIntegral extends QQ`, `ZZ64 extends ZZ`, `NN64 extends ZZ`, `ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, `NN32 extends NN64`, and `Integral[\I\] extends AnyIntegral`. Also `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]` on `TotalComparison` (the prelude's own edit, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:1521-1523`), `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` on `AnyMaybe`, and the five `DistributesOver` markers on `SumReduction` and `ProdReduction`.
26	- **The `excludes` clauses that come**: each integer leaf excludes its integer siblings. `RR64` and `QQ` exclude each other and `AnyIntegral`, as the prelude's `ZZ32 … excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }` does (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`).
27	- **Where the algebra sits**: on the leaves only, as in the prelude. Each integer leaf extends `AnyIntegral` and `Integral[\Self\]`. `Integral[\I\]` extends `StandardTotalOrder[\I\]` and `AdditiveGroup[\I\]`, no longer `AnyIntegral`. `RR64` and `QQ` extend `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, each at their own type. `Number` keeps only the two markers, `AnyAdditiveGroup` and `AnyMultiplicativeRing`. They carry no methods, so the arrays' `excludes AnyMultiplicativeRing` stays true of every number (`FortressLibrary.fss:2195`, `:2503`, `:2670`).
28	- **Why not on `Number` only**: an integer that extends `Integral[\ZZ32\]` gets `Equality[\ZZ32\]` through `StandardTotalOrder`, beside `Number`'s `Equality[\Number\]`. So under "Number only", no integer could be `Integral`. The ranges' bound `I extends Integral[\I\]` (92 lines of `RangeInternals.fsi`) would then admit nothing.
29	- **What `Number` loses**: its operator and function declarations, 52 in the api and 57 in the component, the catch-alls such as `opr +(self, b:Number): RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` (`FortressLibrary.fss:379`). Two reasons, both from the prelude's choice:
30	  - A catch-all applies without coercion to every mixed call. The specification tries coercion only when no declaration applies without it (`conversions-coercions.tex:454-458`), so `x + 1` with `x: ZZ64` would go to float arithmetic, not to `ZZ64`'s `+`.
31	  - The catch-all returns `RR64`. Once `ZZ32` is not below `RR64`, that result breaks the return type rule against each leaf's own `+`.
32	- **Widening**: `coerce` on the wider type. `ZZ64` takes a `ZZ32`; `ZZ` takes the four fixed widths; `NN64` takes an `NN32`. `QQ` and `RR64` take the five integer leaves, and `RR64` also takes a `QQ`. The prelude has the first three groups (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:514-518`, `:575-576`, `:816-817`). It has no coercion from an integer into a float.
33	- **`comprises` clauses**: each leaf comprises its own objects only (`QQ`'s component clause becomes `{ Ratio }`, and the api keeps `{ ... }`), and `Number` has none, as in the prelude. `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32 }` becomes well formed, because the five leaves now extend it directly. 34	- **Methods a leaf inherits today** have to be restated on the leaf, or once on `Integral[\I\]`. The survey of § 2 finds 15 such method names that the tests use.

44	## 1. The return type rule over a chain, and the dispatch change
45	
46	**The sources.** None of them states a rule for a chain.
47	- The specification's Subtype Rule: "If Ps ≺ Qs and Us <: Vs then f(Ps) and f(Qs) are a valid overloading" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:162-166`). It is written for declarations whose static parameters are identical (`:95-96`), so it never meets two instantiations.
48	- Naden's general form, which the checker specialises: "Given a pair of function definitions d2 ≺ d1 in an overload set and a type T to which both are applicable. For every instance of d1 applicable to T with return type R1, there exists an instance of d2 that is applicable to T which has a return type R2 <: R1" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:320-322`).
49	- The checker: it solves for one instance of the generic (`scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:88`) and checks that one arrow (`:97`). Naden's proof says why one is enough under the exclusion rule: it "rules out any instantiation other than the one known at compile time" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:457-460`).
50	
51	Under the forest rule a value is an instance of a self-typed generic at every level of its chain. So Naden's "every instance of d1 applicable to T" is one instance per level. The rule below is his sentence with that set written out. It adds one thing he did not need: a level can be served by a still more specific declaration, because dispatch runs that one there.
52	
53	**The rule, exactly** (`c-full.patch`: `OverloadingOracle.forestLevels` and `forestCovers`, `OverloadingChecker.forestCheck` and `levelDeclares`, `TypeAnalyzer.forestChain`, `TraitTable.declaredNames`). Let f and g be declarations of one name, f more specific than g. Let the stock rule's solution put g's static parameters at A⃗. For every static parameter P of g that is bounded by S[P], with S self-typed, and whose argument A_P is a ground type M:
54	1. The **levels** are the declared non-generic traits and objects L ≠ M with L <: S[L] and L comparable with M: the other points of S's chain through M.
55	2. A level counts when f's domain and g's domain at P := L do not exclude.
56	3. At each counted level, f's return type must be a subtype of g's return type at P := L,
57	4. unless a declaration h is more specific than f and h's domain contains f's domain met with g's domain at P := L. h may be in the overload set, or declared by L itself (a level in another api, like `NN32` in `FortressBuiltin`). In that meet S[L] is read as L when S comprises exactly its parameter: the patents' "the two types include exactly the same sets of values" (US 8,843,887 col. 6 l. 41-55).
58	5. Otherwise the pair is refused: one error per pair, naming the levels.
59	
60	The stock rule still checks M itself. Nothing is checked for a parameter solved to a type variable. That case is two generics with the same parameters, and the call-site fix makes the dispatcher take the call site's argument there. `-Dprobe.identify=true` also reads S[L] as L for an F-bounded S. That is sound only if nothing but L extends S[L], which is what `comprises T` enforces and the F-bound does not: `trait Odd extends { ZZ64, Integral[\ZZ32\] }` is legal under the forest.
61	
62	Two things in the rule were not in the patents note's sketch. Both were found by measuring.
63	- **Levels above count too, not only the levels below.** Where the result holds the parameter invariantly, even a specialisation at the bottom of the chain breaks callers who see the value at a higher level. `ForestLeafInv` has `g(x: Eq[\Narrow\]): Marker[\Narrow\]` beside the generic. It links under the forest alone and dies with `VerifyError: Bad return type`: `Marker⟦Narrow⟧` "is not assignable to" `Marker⟦Wide⟧` (`probes/ForestLeafInv.txt:29-35`). Where the result is covariant in the parameter, the levels above always pass. `X`, `(T,T)` and every tower method are such results.
64	- **The solved level is not the specialisation's own level.** On a chain the solver picks the top. For `ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s methods it picks `ZZ`; for `Number`'s `CMP` and `ZZ64`'s `CMP` beside `StandardPartialOrder`'s it picks `Number` (`deep-errors.txt`, the `M =` list). So "below" is decided per level against f's own domain: L is below f when f's domain, every S[A] read as A, is not inside g's domain at L. Only C-lite uses that distinction; C-full's verdict does not depend on it.
65	
66	**The dispatch change: none beyond the call-site fix.** The patents note expected one. Under the covariant reading the checker can choose the generic's instance at a lower level while the dispatcher still runs the specialisation (`patents-forest-rule.md` § 3, `ForestTowerC` under `cov`). The rule removes that case. It checks every level, so a specialisation whose return type does not fit a lower level is refused, unless something more specific covers that level. And the dispatcher orders declarations with the same oracle (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:524`), so the covariant reading puts the covering declaration first by itself. Measured: `ForestTowerC` is refused under C-full, and `ForestGenericLeaf` and `ForestTowerCLeaf` link and answer right with the dispatcher unchanged (§ 2a).

156	## 3. C-lite: its definition and what it refuses
157	
158	**Definition** (`c-lite.patch`, `-Dprobe.rtr=lite`). The forest rule, and in the return type rule a level below the specialisation is refused outright, whatever the return types. A level above is refused when the return type does not fit. So a specialisation of a generic over a self-typed trait may stand only at a **leaf** of the trait's chain: a level with nothing below it that carries the trait at itself.
159	
160	**Why the leaf.** The patents' dispatch binds a value's parameter at its minimal instance (col. 10 l. 16-17). Only at a leaf is every value that reaches a specialisation at its minimal instance there. At an inner level the specialisation catches values whose callers were promised a lower level, which is the hole; C-full answers that by coverage, and C-lite forbids it. The top of a chain is the worst place for a specialisation, since it catches everything below. So "one level only" can only mean the bottom.

4	
5	**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. Of the 34 that link, 31 have byte-identical classes and 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`). 7	## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today
8	
9	- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
10	- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
11	- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
12	- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
13	- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
14	- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
15	- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). Inside a dispatcher template the arms do this too: they ignore the template's `X`, which the loader has already set to the call site's argument (`javap-excerpts.txt:60-80`).
16	- The authors weighed the question in a comment: "Some overloads have static args, but even if they are supplied, runtime inference is still necessary (so I think) -- drc 2010-02-24 / Not quite so -- if each static parameter is mentioned in any invariant occurrence, then the supplied type is exact" (`OverloadSet.java:1981-1990`).

18	## 2. The design
19	
20	**What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). One set of static arguments, fixed at the call, therefore applies to every declaration. A declaration applies at run time if the value's type is a subtype of its parameter type at those arguments. For `MieDispatchSub`, `grab(b)` with `b: Tag[\Blue\]` fixes `X = Blue`. `Mixed` is not a `Sub[\Blue\]`, so the `Tag` declaration runs and the answer is `Marker[Blue]`.
21	
22	**`MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a)`, `a: Any`.** The specification refuses the program: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)` is an error "for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them" (`overloading.tex:103-105`). The question of which declaration runs therefore does not arise. If the sentence is not enforced, both readings give the same answer. The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. The code should refuse the pair at compile time (§5). Failing that, it should leave the generic arm out of such a dispatcher, which is the `skip` variant below. Either way `grab(a)` returns the `Any` declaration's `Red`.
23	
24	**The three candidates.**
25	- **(a) The dispatcher gains the static arguments as parameters**, and every call site the checker resolved with static arguments pushes their RTTIs. This changes the signature of every dispatcher whose least specific declaration is generic, and the descriptor at every call site that reaches one. The template would then carry `X` twice, in its name and in its parameters. The arms would still be stamped through `loadClosureClass` from RTTI names, which keeps the `ZZ32` naming defect (§4). For `grab(Any)` it passes nothing, because that call site has nothing to pass. Not built.
26	- **(b) The call site loads an instantiated dispatcher named with the static arguments.** It already does, for every dispatcher that is a template (§1). The change is inside the template: each generic arm whose static parameters match the dispatcher's, up to renaming, is renamed into the dispatcher's parameters. It is then tested with a plain `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and called as `grab⟦X⟧` by name, and the loader turns both into `Blue`. Nothing is read from the value, and no signature, call site or template kind changes. This is the specification's model, one instantiation of the name fixed at the call, and it is the smallest of the three. Built.
27	- **(c) The arms keep reading from the value and skip on mismatch.** The template would need `X`'s RTTI in its body. A generic object's RTTI class reads its parameters' RTTIs from fields (`CodeGen.java:5686-5690`), but a function template has no such field, so this needs a new way to name it. Each arm would then compare the RTTI read from the value with it. Equality is wrong where `X` occurs only covariantly, because the value's argument can be a subtype of the call site's. The correct test is "read ⊑ call site" followed by instantiating at the call site's argument, and that is (b) with the reading left in. It changes every generic arm of every template dispatcher, keeps `loadClosureClass`, and keeps both defects of §4. Not built.
